entity.name: John Locke
entity.description: The philosopher who gave America its founding ideas before America existed. His Two Treatises of Government directly shaped Jefferson's Declaration of Independence. Argued the mind begins as a blank slate, championed religious tolerance, and spent five years in political exile writing his masterworks.

story.name: John Locke
story.description: Studies at Oxford during the English Civil War, saves Lord Shaftesbury's life with surgery, flees to the Netherlands in political exile, and returns with Queen Mary to publish three works that reshape Western philosophy.

moments.name: John Locke Is Born to Puritan Parents in Rural Somerset
moments.subtitle: A cloth merchant's grandson in a village that gave no hint of the philosopher he would become
moments.description: On August 29, 1632, John Locke was born in the village of Wrington, Somerset, England, to Puritan parents. His father, John Locke Sr., was an attorney who served as clerk to the Justices of the Peace. The boy was baptized the same day at All Saints' Church. When the English Civil War erupted in 1642, Locke's father fought as a cavalry captain for the Parliamentarian forces under Alexander Popham. That connection changed young Locke's life: in 1647, Popham sponsored the 15-year-old's admission to the prestigious Westminster School in London, launching him from provincial obscurity into the intellectual elite that would shape modern liberalism.

moments.name: Locke Saves Lord Shaftesbury's Life by Coordinating Risky Surgery
moments.subtitle: A philosopher-physician persuades England's most powerful lord to let surgeons cut out a liver cyst
moments.description: In 1668, John Locke faced a medical crisis that cemented his place in English political life. His patron Lord Shaftesbury, then Chancellor of the Exchequer, developed a life-threatening liver infection. Locke, serving as Shaftesbury's personal physician at Exeter House on the Strand in London, coordinated the advice of several doctors and persuaded Shaftesbury to undergo surgery to remove a cyst -- a procedure that was itself potentially fatal in the 17th century. Shaftesbury survived and credited Locke with saving his life. The grateful lord became Locke's most powerful patron, appointing him to governmental positions and drawing him into the political intrigues that would produce Locke's greatest philosophical works.

moments.name: Locke Flees to the Netherlands in Political Exile for Five Years
moments.subtitle: A philosopher on the wrong side of English politics writes his masterworks in hiding
moments.description: In 1683, after his patron Lord Shaftesbury fell from royal favor and died, John Locke fled England for the Netherlands, where he lived in political exile for five years. The English crown suspected Locke of involvement in plots against the monarchy. During this period of exile, Locke composed or completed some of his most important works, including the Essay Concerning Human Understanding and the Two Treatises of Government. He also gained the patronage of Thomas Herbert, 8th Earl of Pembroke. Locke's exile ended dramatically in 1689 when he returned to England aboard the same ship as Queen Mary II following the Glorious Revolution that overthrew King James II.

moments.name: Locke Publishes Three Works That Reshape Western Political Philosophy
moments.subtitle: Written in exile, published anonymously, these books will inspire the American and French revolutions
moments.description: In 1689, shortly after returning from exile in the Netherlands, John Locke published three landmark works: Two Treatises of Government, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, and A Letter Concerning Toleration. The Two Treatises argued that government derives its legitimacy from the consent of the governed and that citizens have the right to revolt against tyranny -- ideas that directly influenced Thomas Jefferson's language in the 1776 Declaration of Independence. The Essay introduced the concept of the mind as a tabula rasa (blank slate), rejecting the notion of innate ideas. All three were published anonymously. Together, they laid the intellectual foundations for modern liberal democracy.

moments.name: Locke Dies at Oates in Essex After 14 Years in a Philosopher's Household
moments.subtitle: The father of liberalism spends his final years in quiet retreat with fellow philosopher Lady Masham
moments.description: On October 28, 1704, John Locke died at Oates, the Essex manor house of Sir Francis and Lady Damaris Masham, where he had lived for the last 14 years of his life. Lady Masham was herself a philosopher whom Locke had known since her youth. Locke had retired from public life due to chronic respiratory illness, but continued writing and corresponding with leading thinkers. He had served as a Commissioner of Trade and Plantations until ill health forced his resignation. Locke was 72. His ideas about natural rights, consent of the governed, and separation of church and state would outlive him by centuries, becoming the bedrock of modern democratic theory.
